facts.statement: The genus is known from a nearly complete skeleton that includes a preserved skull.
facts.quote: Jianchangopterus is known from a nearly complete skeleton with skull preserved.

facts.statement: The fossil was collected from the Tiaojishan Formation.
facts.quote: It was collected from the Tiaojishan Formation.

facts.statement: Lü Junchang and Bo Xue named the genus in 2011 after Jianchang County.
facts.quote: It was first named (after Jianchang County) by Lü Junchang and Bo Xue in 2011

facts.statement: The type species, Jianchangopterus zhaoianus, was named in honor of Zhao Limin, who helped study the only known fossil.
facts.quote: the type species is Jianchangopterus zhaoianus, named for Zhao Limin, who was instrumental in the study of the only known fossil.

facts.statement: The only known fossil is a fully complete skeleton preserved in articulation within a single slab and a counter-slab.
facts.quote: The holotype, and only known fossil, of Jianchangopterus is a fully-complete skeleton preserved in articulation in a single slab with a counter-slab.

facts.statement: The holotype was uncovered at the Linglongta locality in Jianchang County, Liaoning Province, China.
facts.quote: It was uncovered at a locality called Linglongta in Jianchang County in Liaoning Province of China.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is stored at the Yizhou Museum with the catalog number YHK-0931.
facts.quote: The holotype of Jianchangopterus was collected and stored in the Yizhou Museum and was given the specimen number YHK-0931.

facts.statement: Jianchangopterus was a relatively small pterosaur similar in size and shape to Sordes.
facts.quote: Jianchangopterus was a relatively small pterosaur, comparable in both size and morphology to Sordes.

facts.statement: Measurements indicate a skull length of 43 mm and a wingspan of at least 32 cm.
facts.quote: The skull was 43 mm long and the combined length of the arm and finger bones was about 162 mm, which translates to a wingspan of at least 32 cm.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Jianchangopterus likely ate insects, unlike most of its contemporaries which ate fish.
facts.quote: The authors of its description remark that it most likely ate insects, whereas most of the other pterosaurs it lived with likely ate fish.

facts.statement: The genus is classified in the family Rhamphorhynchidae and the subfamily Scaphognathinae.
facts.quote: Jianganchopterus was assigned to the family Rhamphorhynchidae and the subfamily Scaphognathinae by Lü and Bo.

facts.statement: Classification is based on shared traits such as a short skull, short wing finger, long fifth toe, and long ulna.
facts.quote: They made this assignment based on the presence of several synapomorphies of scaphognathines shared by Jianchangopterus including a relatively short skull, a relatively short wing finger, a long fifth toe, and a relatively long ulna.

facts.statement: It is considered a close relative of Sordes, Scaphognathus, Harpactognathus, and Fenghuangopterus.
facts.quote: The authors remarked that it is likely a close relative of Sordes, while also being closely related to Scaphognathus, Harpactognathus, and Fenghuangopterus.

facts.statement: The fossil dates to the Callovian-Oxfordian age of the Middle-Late Jurassic, approximately 159 million years ago.
facts.quote: The only known Jianchangopterus fossil was found in rocks assigned to the Tiaojishan Formation, dating to the Callovian-Oxfordian age of the Middle-Late Jurassic, dated to approximately 159 million years ago.

facts.statement: The environment featured forests surrounding large lakes near active volcanoes, where volcanic ash aided fossil preservation.
facts.quote: These forests surrounded large lakes in the shadow of active volcanoes, ash from which was responsible for the remarkable preservation of many of the fossils.

facts.statement: The climate was likely subtropical to temperate, warm, and humid.
facts.quote: Based on the Tiajishan's plant life, its climate would have been subtropical to temperate, warm and humid.

facts.statement: The time range extends from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian, between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Kimmeridgian (168.2 to 152.21 million years ago)
